title: The Slow Wardrobe
premise: Juniper Sandoval, a translator whose childhood language is dissolving word by word into borrowed English, returns to their hometown when the house where they were raised goes up at auction. Sorting the estate, they discover photographs of a stranger who lived with the family for a year — a runaway their parents sheltered and never mentioned. As Juniper pieces together why the family kept this secret, they must decide whether to bid on a house that holds both tenderness and betrayal. In the end, Juniper lets the house go but claims the story, translating their mother's unsent letters and finding that forgiveness is a language you can learn late.
about_author: Orsen Underhill is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent fifteen years listening to other people's most carefully chosen words. They write about inheritance, silence, and the houses we can't go home to.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. A translator in the city, Juniper catalogs the words of their childhood language they can no longer recall, keeping lists like a person counting losses. News arrives: the family house is up for auction after their mother's death. The emotional beat is quiet dread — grief arriving as paperwork, and the fear that returning will confirm how much has already been lost.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photographs
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Clearing the house before the auction, Juniper finds photos of an unknown young woman at their kitchen table, dated the year their father left. Neighbors remember 'the girl who stayed.' Juniper confronts their aunt, who reveals only fragments: the girl was fleeing something, and the mother hid her at real cost. The beat is destabilized identity — the childhood home contained a life Juniper never knew.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, intercut with the found letters. At the auction, Juniper discovers the girl — now a middle-aged woman named Rosa — has come back too, hoping to buy the house that once saved her. Bidding turns personal; a developer outbids them both. In the aftermath, Rosa gives Juniper the letters their mother wrote in the fading language. The climax lands as justice outside any courtroom: two strangers choosing truth over ownership.

chapters.title: What the House Kept
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Sitting in the emptied house one last night before the new owners arrive, Juniper translates the letters slowly, recovering words they thought were gone. They forgive the mother who hid so much, and Rosa becomes something like family — not by blood or address, but by shared custody of a story. The resolution: loss remains, but language, like love, can be rebuilt from what survives.
